glossary.meaning: In Cassian's Marseilles, the help of God without which no effort reaches its goal. Grace "always co-operates with our will," and "assists, protects, and defends it." Which one began the good, grace or the will, we left open. We held grace together with a free will on purpose - in a relation "that cannot be fully grasped by the mind and reason of man."

At Tours, virtus is not first a moral quality but effective power. It is the "power present" Martin feels before he raises the dead, and the "abundance of power" he had as a monk and had less of as a bishop. At Marseilles Cassian uses the same word for moral virtue, and declines on principle to "weave a tale of God's miracles and signs."

In Cassian's Marseilles, discretion is the virtue by which every other is kept from destroying itself. It is "the mother of all virtues, as well as their guardian and regulator," the "eye and light of the body," the "royal road" between excess and slackness. It is gained "only ... by true humility." That means testing every thought, like a good money-changer testing coin, against the judgment of the elders.

The picture that governed a monk's life among us. A man had changed service - from Caesar's army, or from a worldly career - to Christ's. He now stood girded, under oath, in daily combat against the devil and his own faults. The one who slackened was, in Cassian's word, a deserter.
Vincent's book. By its own name it is an aid to memory, against his own forgetting. He signs it "Peregrinus, the least of all the servants of God" - a teller, not an author.

pull_quotes.speaker_or_author: Vincent, presbyter of the island, who wrote as Peregrinus
pull_quotes.text: In God there is one substance but three Persons. In Christ there are two substances but one Person.

The Lord Jesus never said he would come back dressed in purple, with a glittering crown on his head. I will not believe Christ has come unless he comes looking the way he did when he suffered, and openly shows the marks of his wounds from the cross.

pull_quotes.speaker_or_author: one of the elders of Egypt, unnamed, as Cassian reports him (Institutes V.24)
pull_quotes.text: I can fast any day. But I am about to walk you on your way, and I will not have you with me for long. A fast is good and worth doing, but it is a gift I choose to give. Charity is a command, and a command has to be carried out. So since I receive Christ in you, I ought to feed him. Once I have sent you on, I can make up for the welcome I gave for his sake by fasting more strictly on my own. For "the bridegroom's friends cannot fast while the bridegroom is with them." But once he has gone, then they will rightly fast.

cite.text: The monks and clergy of Marseilles and Lerins were "the Massilians" - "the remnants of the Pelagians," the semi-Pelagian party - a school of one doctrine, opposed to predestination, that Cassian, Vincent, and Faustus alike held and that Rome condemned.

exchange.speaker: participant
exchange.text: Did you believe people are saved by faith alone, not works?

exchange.speaker: representative
exchange.text: Neither half of that is the shape our own life gave the question. Hear it as a brother heard it. Among the brethren at Marseilles a monk fasts, watches, keeps his cell, and lays every thought bare to the senior. At the moment he feels the fast has done something, he is taught to say that it was not he, but the grace of God with him. Both halves are commanded. Cassian set it down as the elders' teaching, not his own: perfection cannot be gained without these labours, and by these labours alone, without the grace of God, no one can attain it. The will always remains free in a man; and it is weak; and the help of God is needed by it every day and hour. The argument came to us as a story. Two friends came back to morning service in Egypt troubled by one sentence an old man had added the night before - that a man cannot make himself master of the good by his own toil. The elder saw them whispering, cut the psalms short, and answered with a field. The husbandman ploughs and still needs the rain. He cannot ascribe the crop to himself. And God does not send rich crops to the idle. That morning the elder drew one conclusion. The start even of our good thoughts comes from God, who first stirs a good will in us. Our part is to follow, humbly, day by day, the grace that draws us. Later in the same teaching he put it the other way as well. Two things we refused. We refused the notion that gives everything to the will and hands out grace by a man's deserts; Vincent, on the island, named Pelagius for it. And we refused, as grievous blasphemy, the thought that God does not will all men to be saved. How both are true - how God works all things in us and yet everything can be ascribed to free will - cannot be fully grasped by the mind and reason of man. We stopped there, where the fathers stopped. If you ask which side we stood on, our teacher would not answer that with a formula. He kept both sides in one sentence.

cite.text: To stop tribunes from hunting heretics in the Spains, Martin takes communion once with the bishops he had refused. An angel tells him his remorse is just. He feels his power lessened, and he never attends a synod again.

exchange.speaker: participant
exchange.text: Your church used power against Christians who disagreed. Defend that.

exchange.speaker: representative
exchange.text: Our own saint did not defend it, and he was there. This is what happened. A synod of bishops had condemned a man and his followers as heretics in their absence, and the affair went from the bishops to the emperor's court at Treves. The accuser there was himself a bishop, and the bishops gathered in the city were daily in communion with him and had made common cause with him. The condemned man was put to death. Then worse was being prepared: tribunes with power of life and death were to be sent into the Spains to hunt out heretics, and a man was counted one for turning pale, or for the clothes he wore. Martin went to the court to stop it. He held that the bishops had done enough when they declared men heretics and put them out of the churches, and that a secular ruler sitting as judge in a cause of the Church was a foul and unheard-of thing. He went, Sulpitius says, to protect even heretics themselves. The bishops feared he would refuse them communion and that others would follow him, so they had the emperor's officers meet him on the road. When persuasion failed, the emperor grew angry, and executioners were named for the men Martin was pleading for. That night Martin ran to the palace and pledged that he would take communion with those bishops if the men were spared and the tribunes recalled. It was granted. He took the communion once, judging it better to yield for an hour than to let the sword fall. He left the city in grief, sat alone in a wood accusing and defending what he had done, and afterward, when he cured the possessed more slowly than before, confessed with tears that he felt his power lessened by that communion. He lived sixteen years more and never went to a synod again. So the sword was drawn in the Church's cause among us, by bishops. The man we remember is the one who yielded once to stop it, and grieved over it afterward. We do not defend it, and the man at the centre of it never called it right. Two limits belong with it. The accuser is heard only through the man who called him worthless. And on the island Vincent, in his own voice, held that one who preaches other than what was received is to be cut off, lest one sick sheep infect the flock. He looked to an ancient council as the guard of the faith. Our two houses never argued any of this with each other.

cite.text: Purity of heart as the goal, discretion as its regulator, the eight faults as its combats - what Cassian wrote out for the monks of Gaul from the Fathers: 'the immediate aim or goal, is purity of heart, without which no one can gain that end' (Conf. I.4); fastings, vigils, and renunciation 'are not perfection, but aids to perfection' (I.7); 'discretion is the mother of all virtues, as well as their guardian and regulator' (II.4); the eight faults 'and the remedies for them according to their traditions' (Inst. Pref.); vainglory that 'creates a wish to take holy orders' (Inst. XI.14). In Tours, the thing appears without the vocabulary. Martin sees through Anatolius's robe and the purple-robed 'Christ' (Vita XXIII-XXIV). But there is no talk of purity of heart, no discretion, no list of faults. Cassian frames every element of this program as received from Egypt, not his own invention; what Gaul contributed was the adaptation - carried west and adapted for a colder climate (Inst. I.10, IV.10-11), its severity sustained by a real fear of spiritual cooling. The English edition this account draws on leaves out two of Cassian's conferences on this program: XII, on chastity, and XXII, on nocturnal illusions. It also leaves out Institutes VI.

exchange.speaker: participant
exchange.text: What did your way of life offer someone who struggled to quiet their own mind?

exchange.speaker: representative
exchange.text: A mill that cannot stop, and a choice of what it grinds. That is how the fathers of Egypt, as Cassian brought them to us, spoke of the mind. Thoughts will come; a man cannot keep them from rising. What lies in his power is to admit them or to turn them away. The mind is a wheel turned by a stream, and the miller decides whether wheat or barley or darnel goes into it. So among the brethren at Marseilles the life was built to keep the wheel fed. The psalms learned by heart and said at the work. Twelve psalms at evening and twelve at night, received from the fathers, so that a man who would otherwise let the whole day pass without prayer is held to it by a rule. Labour in the cell without ceasing, so that the wandering heart, fastened within the barriers of the cell as in a secure harbour, is held still. And a lesson taught early: every itching thought was laid bare to the senior as soon as it rose, before it was acted on. A thought we are ashamed to tell is from the devil, and a wrong thought loses its strength the moment it is discovered. The fathers knew the hour the mind revolts, too. About the sixth hour a monk comes to hate his cell, finds the brethren contemptible, goes in and out, watches the sun as if it were slow to set, and finds a pious reason to leave. They called it accidie, and their remedy was to stay. All of it served one mark. The end of the life is the kingdom; the nearer goal is purity of heart, a heart cleared to charity, and the archer fixes his gaze on that mark or cannot tell whether his aim improves. Every fast and vigil is ranked by whether it clears the heart - an aid, never the point. At Tours the words were not used, but the thing was there: the saint kept his mind on prayer even at other work, the way a smith beats his anvil between strokes.

cite.text: A citizen lures a monk out of his monastery by pretending his wife is ill. The monk is taken to the city under a kind of guard. Some bishops object to his mean clothes and his hair. A psalm read at random answers them.

The monk-bishop came to office as a captive, never as a candidate. Martin was drawn from his monastery by a trick and made bishop of Tours by the one wish of all the people, over the impious resistance of a few bishops whose only objection was that his clothing was mean and his hair disgusting, and the objectors were confounded by a psalm; the same shape holds at every house - Honoratus overtaken by the dignity he fled, Archebius "carried off" - so that nobody in this world's own stories wanted the see.

exchange.speaker: participant
exchange.text: Who chose your leaders — were bishops appointed, elected, or something else?

exchange.speaker: representative
exchange.text: Something else. Among us the office was not sought; it came for the man who had fled it. This is how it came at Tours. Martin could not easily be drawn out of his monastery, so a citizen named Ruricius threw himself at his knees and pretended his wife was ill. Crowds had been posted along the road, and he was escorted to the city under a kind of guard. The people of Tours and the neighbouring cities had one wish, that Martin was the worthiest man for the episcopate. A few of the bishops summoned to make the appointment resisted, saying his person was contemptible, his clothing mean, and his hair disgusting. The reader for the day was blocked out by the crowd, so a bystander seized the psalter and read the first verse he found - praise perfected out of the mouths of babes, to destroy the enemy and the avenger - and the people took it as a verdict on the objectors. Then the new bishop kept a monk's habits inside the office. On the island, as far as the sermon on Honoratus can be read, the office came to its founder when he was made a presbyter: he who had refused to go to the dignity, the dignity came to him. No house wrote of another's. And the one Egyptian bishop Cassian chose to tell us of, Archebius, had been carried off from the anchorites and given to a town as its bishop, and complained that he had been expelled from the monastic life as unworthy of it. Our own teaching made wanting the office a fault. The fathers of Egypt taught that vainglory creates a wish for holy orders, and that the man who wants to rule others has grown cold through pride. So no one in our stories wanted the see. Hear the limit of that. Every one of those stories is a house's own telling of its own founder. Sulpitius was not present at the election, and he was no friend to the bishops who objected. Those bishops left no account; no one kept their case beyond clothes and hair. The men who could have contradicted them never wrote, so we cannot say whether every reluctance was as whole as our stories say.

quiet.statement: If you dug up the places we lived, we could not tell you what you would find. Not the caves and the wooden cell across the river from Tours. Not the island in its harbour. Not the two houses at Marseilles. Nothing we can hand you comes out of the ground. All of it comes from books: one man's Life of the saint, with his letters and his dialogues; Cassian's Institutes, written for a bishop's new house, and his book of the elders' talks; Vincent's remembrancer; a funeral sermon for the island's founder; and a list of authors written down a generation after us. Even the names you may know for our places are not in our own books, so we do not use them. What we can tell you of daily life comes from what Cassian said Egypt did. It also comes from his complaint that no one in Gaul kept it up unbroken even a year, and from what Sulpitius said the saint did in his cell. Of the island's own day, not a line. What we ate, where we slept, what the rooms looked like - only as far as those pages say, and no further.

dates.display: d. 397, on a peacemaking journey to Condate; a soldier under 'Julian Caesar' in his youth, discharged at a donative; monk 'not far from the town' where Hilary was bishop, then bishop of Tours from an undated election (the monastery across the river founded 'after 371' only on the editorial introduction's word); 'lived sixteen years' after the Treves affair by Gallus's own reckoning

writing c. 397 (the Life; Letter III within months of Martin's death) to c. 404-406 (the Dialogues); an Aquitanian 'of an illustrious family' who visited Martin at Tours; birth and death years rest only on the modern editors' disagreeing endnotes and are not asserted

travelled in Egypt with Germanus in his youth (the interval to his writing not stated in this world's own documents); founded the twin houses at Marseilles c. 415; wrote the Institutes for Castor before 426 and the Conferences in three parts, Part II (to Honoratus and Eucherius) not later than 426; d. c. 435

names.name: Cassian, the founder of the houses at Marseilles

dates.display: founded the community on the island of Lerins c. 400-410 (410 on the surviving volume's editorial introduction); addressed by Cassian as a brother presiding over a large monastery, then as a bishop - the see identified as Arles, from 426, only by the editorial apparatus; d. c. 429/430, the year his disciple and successor Hilary preached his life

names.name: Honoratus, the founder of the island
Honoratus of Lerins, later bishop of Arles (d. c. 429/430)

who_speaks.text: Four figures carry the voice of the two households. Martin was the soldier who left the army for Christ and was drawn out of his monastery to be made a bishop. Sulpitius Severus admired him and wrote almost everything known about him, much of it from what Martin and his brothers told him. Cassian lived among Egypt's monks and carried their teaching to Marseilles. In his Institutes he chose not to write of wonders. Honoratus founded a community on an island of snakes. There, as far as his disciple's sermon can be read, the priesthood he had fled caught up with him.

documented_stories.teaser: A soldier cuts his cloak in two for a naked beggar at the city gate. That night, Sulpitius says, he sees Christ in his sleep, wearing the half he gave away.
documented_stories.tellable_as: A catechumen soldier has nothing left but his cloak. He cuts it in two for a naked beggar at a city gate. That night he sees Christ wearing the half he gave away.
documented_stories.telling:
Martin's father was a tribune, an army officer. When Martin was fifteen, his father informed on him, and he was seized, put in chains and made to swear the soldier's oath. Even then he kept only one servant, and Martin was the one who served, pulling off his servant's boots and cleaning them himself. He was still a catechumen, preparing for baptism, and he kept from his pay only what each day required.

One winter was so harsh that many people were dying of the cold. At the gate of Amiens, Martin met a poor man with no clothes at all, and everyone passed him by. Martin had nothing left but his weapons and his cloak. He drew his sword, cut the cloak in two, and gave half to the beggar. Some onlookers laughed at him, while others were ashamed, because they had more than he did and had never done anything like it.

That night, Sulpitius tells us, Martin saw Christ in his sleep, wearing the half he had given away. Christ told the angels around him that Martin, still only a catechumen, had clothed him. Martin did not grow proud, and he went and was baptized at twenty. His commander, a tribune who shared his tent, promised to leave the world with him once his own command ended. So Martin stayed nearly two more years, a soldier in name only.
documented_stories.title: Half a Cloak at the Gate of Amiens
documented_stories.when: While Martin was still a soldier and not yet baptized; the text gives no year

documented_stories.teaser: Called a coward for refusing to fight, a soldier offers to face the enemy unarmed. The next day, the enemy asks for peace.
documented_stories.tellable_as: At a donative before a battle, a soldier tells Caesar he is now the soldier of Christ and may not fight. He offers to stand unarmed before the enemy. The next day the enemy asks for peace.
documented_stories.telling:
Barbarians were pushing into Gaul, and Julian Caesar had gathered his army to meet them. He was handing out a donative, a gift of money, and calling his soldiers forward one by one. When Martin's turn came, he would not take the money. He had served Caesar long enough, he said, and now he asked to serve God. As Christ's soldier, it was not lawful for him to fight.

Julian, whom Sulpitius calls the tyrant, said Martin was running from the coming battle out of fear. The charge only made Martin firmer. If this was cowardice, he said, he would stand before the enemy line the next day with no weapon. The sign of the cross would be his only protection. He was sent back to prison to wait for morning.

The next day the enemy sent envoys to ask for peace. Sulpitius tells us God was sparing Martin the sight of other men dying. The enemy gave up themselves and everything they had, and no battle was fought.
documented_stories.title: Martin Asks Caesar for His Discharge
documented_stories.when: Before a battle in Gaul, when Martin left the army; the text gives no year

documented_stories.teaser: Martin returns to find a new believer dead before baptism. He bolts the door and stretches himself over the body. Sulpitius says that two hours later the man opens his eyes.
documented_stories.tellable_as: Martin returns to find a catechumen dead and unbaptized. He bolts the door and stretches himself on the body. He perceives that power is present, and two hours later the man opens his eyes. Afterward the man tells of the tribunal and the two angels that sent him back.
documented_stories.telling:
Martin had set up a monastery for himself not far from the town. A catechumen, a man still preparing for baptism, came to live with him and learn from his teaching and his life. Within a few days the man fell ill with fever. Martin was away for three days, and when he came back the man was dead, so suddenly that he had never been baptized.

As Sulpitius tells it, Martin sent everyone out of the cell, bolted the door and stretched himself full length on the body. He prayed, and when he sensed that power was present, he rose and waited for the Lord's mercy. Within two hours the dead man began to stir and opened his eyes. Martin cried out his thanks so loudly that the brothers rushed in and found alive the man they had left dead. He was baptized at once and lived for many years.

He used to tell us what had happened to him. He had stood before the Judge and been sent to a gloomy place among common crowds. Then two angels said that he was the man Martin was praying for, and he was given back to Martin. From that day, people counted Martin holy, powerful and truly apostolic.
documented_stories.title: Martin Brings a Dead Catechumen Back
documented_stories.when: After Martin left the army and set up his monastery; the text gives no year

documented_stories.teaser: A citizen pretends his wife is sick to draw a monk from his monastery. Some bishops object to his shabby clothes and hair. A psalm opened at random answers them.
documented_stories.tellable_as: A citizen lures a monk out of his monastery by pretending his wife is ill. The monk is taken to the city under a kind of guard. Some bishops object to his mean clothes and his hair. A psalm read at random answers them.
documented_stories.telling:
The people of Tours wanted Martin as their bishop, but Sulpitius says he could not easily be drawn out of his monastery. So a citizen named Ruricius knelt before him and pretended that his wife was sick. When Martin came out to help, citizens lining the road led him into the city as if under guard. A huge crowd from Tours and the nearby towns had gathered to vote, and nearly all of them wanted Martin.

A few people objected, among them some of the bishops called in to consecrate him. Led by a bishop named Defensor, they said Martin looked contemptible, with his shabby clothes and disgusting hair. The crowd only laughed.

That day the reader could not get through the crowd. While the officials stood confused, someone picked up the psalter and read the first verse he found. Out of the mouths of babes and infants, it said, God had perfected praise, to destroy the enemy and the avenger. The crowd roared, and Defensor's side fell silent, for people believed God had chosen the verse as a witness against him. Martin became our bishop, and as bishop he kept the dignity of the office and the plain habits of a monk.
documented_stories.title: The Monk Lured Out to Be Made Bishop
documented_stories.when: Years after Martin's discharge; the text gives no year

documented_stories.teaser: To save lives, a bishop takes communion with men he had refused. In return, the officers sent to hunt heretics in Spain are called back. He never goes to a synod again.
documented_stories.tellable_as: To stop tribunes from hunting heretics in the Spains, Martin takes communion once with the bishops he had refused. An angel tells him his remorse is just. He feels his power lessened, and he never attends a synod again.
documented_stories.telling:
We have this story from Gallus, one of Martin's disciples, in Sulpitius's Dialogues. Martin never told it outside his own household.

After Priscillian was put to death, the emperor Maximus protected Ithacius, the bishop who had accused him. The bishops gathered at Trier stood by Ithacius. Maximus was about to send tribunes, officers with power over life and death, into Spain to hunt down heretics. Martin came to court and begged that none be sent, to spare the heretics as well as the true Christians. In his Sacred History, Sulpitius tells of an earlier stage, before Priscillian's death. There he says Martin held it a shocking wrong for a worldly ruler to judge a church case.

The bishops begged Maximus to turn against Martin, and Maximus ordered death for the people Martin had defended. Martin hurried to the palace that night and promised to take communion with the bishops if those lives were spared and the tribunes called back. Maximus agreed. The next day, when a bishop named Felix was ordained, Martin took communion, yet he would never put his name to it in writing.

Leaving the city, he sat alone in the woods near the village of Andethanna, torn with grief. Gallus says an angel came and told him his remorse was just, though he had no other way out. Afterward his healing sometimes came more slowly, and with tears Martin blamed that one communion. Gallus says he lived sixteen more years and never went to a synod again.
documented_stories.title: Martin Yields Once, at the Emperor's Court
documented_stories.when: After Priscillian was put to death, while Maximus ruled at Trier; the text gives no year

documented_stories.teaser: A priest Martin raised from boyhood rages at him, then soon comes back to beg pardon. Martin will not remove him. If Christ bore with Judas, why not Brictio?
documented_stories.tellable_as: A presbyter Martin raised from boyhood storms into the courtyard. He calls his master's visions ridiculous fancies, then soon comes back and begs pardon. Martin will not remove him: if Christ bore with Judas, why should he not bear with Brictio?
documented_stories.telling:
One day Martin sat on his wooden seat, the one we all knew, in the little court outside his door. Gallus says Martin saw two demons on the rock above the monastery, calling out with glee, "Come here, Brictio, come here, Brictio." Then Brictio burst in, raging.

Brictio was a presbyter, a priest, whom Martin had raised in the monastery from boyhood. The day before, Martin had rebuked him, because Brictio had owned nothing when he joined the clergy and was now buying horses and slaves. Many said the slaves included boys bought from beyond the frontier and girls chosen for their looks. Pale with fury, Brictio claimed he was the holier man, since he had grown up in the Church while Martin had been a soldier. He called Martin's visions ridiculous fancies and nearly struck him, but Martin answered him gently.

Brictio stormed out, sure he had won. Soon he came back, threw himself at Martin's feet and begged for pardon, admitting that a demon had taken hold of him. Martin forgave him easily. Afterward, whenever Brictio was accused of serious wrongs, Martin would not remove him. He did not want anyone to think he was avenging an insult to himself. If Christ bore with Judas, he would ask, why should he not bear with Brictio?
documented_stories.title: If Christ Bore with Judas
documented_stories.when: Undated; told in Sulpitius's Dialogues, about 404 to 406

documented_stories.teaser: Knowing his end is near, Martin goes to make peace among quarreling clergy. Dying, he turns down straw for sackcloth and ashes, so as not to leave a different example.
documented_stories.tellable_as: Foreknowing his death, Martin goes to make peace among quarrelling clerics. He sickens, and refuses straw for his bed of sackcloth and ashes rather than set his disciples a softer example. At his funeral, it is said, nearly two thousand monks gather, old men and young soldiers of Christ, with a choir of virgins.
documented_stories.telling:
Martin had long known when he would die, Sulpitius writes, and he had told the brothers so. When the clergy at Condate fell to quarreling, he went to make peace among them. One more church at peace, he judged, would be a fitting end to his life.

Peace was made, but as he was about to return to the monastery, his strength failed. The brothers wept and begged him not to leave them, and Martin wept too. He prayed that he would not refuse more work if he was still needed, and he left the choice to God.

For some days he lay in fever on sackcloth and ashes, praying through whole nights. When his disciples asked to put some ordinary straw under him, he refused. A Christian should die among ashes, he said, and he would be sinning if he left them a different example. Those who were there told us that he saw the devil standing near and rebuked him without fear. Then he died, and they said his face looked like an angel's.

The whole city his body was brought to poured out to meet it, with people from the villages and towns around. Almost two thousand monks, it is said, came to his funeral. Old men walked with young soldiers of Christ, and a choir of virgins kept their grief hidden.
documented_stories.title: Martin Refuses the Straw

documented_stories.teaser: Egyptian fathers cannot agree how many psalms to sing each evening. At the hour of prayer, Cassian reports, one father sings twelve and vanishes. They take twelve as the number.
documented_stories.tellable_as: The fathers of Egypt argue whether the daily psalms should be fifty or sixty. The Vesper hour interrupts them. One father rises to sing, finishes the twelfth psalm with Alleluia, and vanishes. The number is fixed forever, not by any monk but by an angel.
documented_stories.telling:
Cassian brought us this story from the fathers of Egypt. In the earliest days, they say, only a few men were called monks, and they were the best of men. They lived like the first believers in Jerusalem, with one heart and one soul and everything shared. The elder fathers met to set a daily rule of prayer for those who would come after them.

Each father thought only of his own strength and proposed the number of psalms that suited him. Some wanted fifty, some sixty and some still more, and they were still arguing when the hour for evening prayer came.

So they stopped to pray. One father rose to sing while the rest sat listening, and he sang eleven psalms, each followed by a prayer. Then he ended the twelfth with Alleluia and vanished from their sight. The fathers saw Providence at work, for through an angel, they believed, a rule had been fixed for every community of brothers. From then on they kept twelve psalms at the evening and night prayers, and later they added two readings of their own choosing.
documented_stories.title: The Angel Who Set the Number of Psalms
documented_stories.when: Set in the early days of Egypt's monks, no year given; Cassian wrote it down in Gaul

documented_stories.teaser: Two friends come to morning prayer troubled by something an old monk said the night before. He cuts the service short and answers with a farmer who still needs rain.
documented_stories.tellable_as: Two friends come back to morning prayer troubled by one sentence an old man added the night before: no one masters the good by his own toil. The old man cuts the office short. He answers with a farmer who still needs the rain.
documented_stories.telling:
Cassian wrote this down years later, in Gaul. He and his friend Germanus had spent an evening hearing an old man named Chaeremon teach on chastity, at his cell near Panephysis in Egypt. One sentence troubled Germanus. The old man had said that even striving with all one's might cannot make a person master of the good. That must be received as a gift.

They slept a little and came back for morning prayer, still whispering about it. Chaeremon noticed, cut the service short and asked what was wrong.

Germanus said that chastity is won by long, hard toil. The credit should go mainly to the one who does the work, as a farmer earns his harvest. Chaeremon answered that no farmer can claim his harvest by his labor alone, because he needs rain he cannot control. Yet God gives no rich crop to a farmer who never plows. In the same way, the wish to do good and the chance to do it both come first from God. Our part, he said, is to follow day by day the grace that draws us on.

Later in the same Conference, Chaeremon says that grace works together with our will, and sometimes waits for some effort from it. Elsewhere he says that wanting the good, doing it and holding on to it are all God's gifts. Yet none of them takes away free will, and how both are true, he says, the human mind cannot fully grasp.
documented_stories.title: The Farmer Who Still Needs the Rain
documented_stories.when: Set in Egypt, no year given; Cassian wrote it down in Gaul, not later than 426

documented_stories.teaser: A founder walks unafraid onto an island shunned for its filth and snakes, a psalm on his lips. His disciple Hilary says the snakes gave way.
documented_stories.tellable_as: Hilary tells how Honoratus went unafraid onto an island shunned for its filth and its serpents, with a psalm on his lips. The serpents gave way, and a camp of God rose there. There, as far as his sermon can be read, the priest's headband caught the man who had run from it.
documented_stories.telling:
When our founder Honoratus died, his disciple and successor Hilary preached his life. Honoratus, Hilary says, left his homeland because he longed for the desert. There was an island that stood empty, because it was filthy and no one could go near it for fear of poisonous snakes. He was drawn there by the chance of solitude, and by the nearness of the holy bishop Leontius, whom he loved. Many people tried to hold him back by warning him how terrible the place was. But he wanted to be cut off from the world, even by the sea.

He carried a psalm in his heart and on his lips. It promised that he would tread on the asp and the basilisk, and trample the lion and the dragon. So he went in unafraid, Hilary says, and his calm scattered the fear of his own people. The horror of the empty place fled, and the snakes gave way. Snakes were often met in those parts, Hilary adds, yet they never harmed or even frightened anyone, and he counts this among his master's miracles.

There Honoratus set up a camp of God. And there, as far as Hilary's sermon can be read, the priesthood caught up with the man who had run from it. He was made a presbyter, a priest, and he kept a monk's humility inside the priesthood.
documented_stories.title: Honoratus and the Island of Snakes
documented_stories.when: Told in a funeral sermon by his successor at Arles; the text gives no year

floor_note.text: The two households confessed what the wider Church confessed about Christ, and they treated it as settled. Vincent, writing on the island, gave the faith in one formula. In God there is one substance but three Persons, and in Christ two substances but one Person. He used it as an example of his rule, that the true faith is what has been believed everywhere, always, by everyone. One man had wanted Mary called the mother of Christ but not the mother of God. The bishops at Ephesus refused him, three years before Vincent wrote.

highlights.note: The Aquitanian who wrote the Life of Martin. He says he learned it partly from Martin and partly from those who lived with him.
Sulpitius calls him only Julian Caesar. An editor today says he was Julian the Apostate. The Life of Martin never says so.
A man put to death after the bishop Ithacius accused him. Sulpitius, who was hostile to him, sums up the charges in his Sacred History.

highlights.label: Maximus
highlights.note: The emperor was Maximus. At Trier he took the side of Ithacius, the man who had accused Priscillian.

highlights.label: Postumianus
highlights.note: This is Postumianus, a speaker in the Dialogues. His praise of Martin is in words Sulpitius wrote.
highlights.phrase: a traveler just back from Egypt

highlights.note: An old man whose cell stood near Panephysis in Egypt. Years later, in Gaul, Cassian set down his teaching in Cassian's own words.
A meeting of bishops. After Trier, Martin stayed away from them. Vincent of Lérins trusted an ancient general council's decrees to guard the faith.
Fellowship in the church, and the sacrament within it. To withhold it was the church's sharpest penalty. Martin felt that one forced communion weakened his power.
A coarse robe. Martin wore it to pray, to cast out demons and to die in. Cassian's Egyptian fathers refused it as too showy.
The Egyptian fathers' word, passed on by Cassian, for the judgment that keeps each virtue from going wrong. A monk gained it through humility.
The monk's nearest goal, short of heaven itself. Cassian's Egyptian fathers ranked fasting and night prayer as aids to it, never the point.
God's help, without which no effort reaches its goal. Scholars still disagree on whether Cassian held that grace or the will begins the good.
Women who had taken a consecrated state, with its own dress. No woman among them is named, and none speaks.
People judged to have left the ancient, universal church. Martin held that bishops might expel them, but an emperor's sword had no place.
The city of Tours in France, where Martin became bishop. The Romans knew it as Caesarodunum.
Greek Massalia, founded around 600 BCE, now Marseille in France. Cassian is said to have founded two houses here, one for men, one for women.
The island is now Île Saint-Honorat, off the coast of France. Honoratus founded a monastery there.
Roman Samarobriva, now the city of Amiens in France. Martin met the beggar at its gate.
A Roman city, now Trier in Germany. The emperor Maximus held his court there.
The settlement where Martin went to make peace among the clergy of its church, and where he died. It is probably today's Candes-Saint-Martin in France.
A village near Trier where Martin sat grieving in the woods. It is probably Niederanven in Luxembourg, though an editor calls the text corrupt.
A town in Egypt, at what is now el-Manzala. The old man's cell stood near it.

legacy.text: After 450 the argument over grace and effort went on, but it was no longer one monk writing to another. In the 470s Faustus, once abbot of Lérins and by then a bishop, took it up. He says he wrote at the request of church councils at Arles and Lyons, as a bishop writing for other bishops.

read_first.note: Martin's life from soldier to bishop, by a man who knew him and heard the stories from Martin and his brothers.

source.citation: Sulpitius Severus, On the Life of St. Martin (Vita Martini), trans. Alexander Roberts, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, 2nd series, vol. 11, ed. Schaff and Wace

read_first.note: Egypt's customs, set down for a new house in Gaul and changed only where Gaul's climate or habits made them too hard.

source.citation: John Cassian, The Twelve Books on the Institutes of the Coenobia, trans. Edgar C. S. Gibson, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, 2nd series, vol. 11, ed. Schaff and Wace

read_first.note: A short book written as a rule for telling true growth in the faith from a corruption dressed up as one.

source.citation: Vincent of Lerins, The Commonitory, trans. C. A. Heurtley, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, 2nd series, vol. 11, ed. Schaff and Wace

relations_summary.text: Martin's household grew up in a church torn by heresy. Sulpitius says Martin found the church in Gaul in turmoil, because heretics had driven the bishop Hilary into exile. At Milan, a man named Auxentius drove Martin out as well, and he went to live on a small island. When Hilary came home, Martin followed him and built a monastery near his town.

sourcing.text: Most of what survives is one man's account of another. Sulpitius Severus wrote about Martin, and Cassian wrote down what Egypt's monks taught him. Both households wrote much about virtue. Tours also wrote of Martin's power, while Cassian set down Egypt's customs more than the days of his own houses. The island's daily life is known least of all, and the books from Tours do not say what the brothers sang or when. Both houses kept communities of women, yet no woman's own words survive. Cassian's English translator also left out three of his texts on the body and its discipline.

story.text: In Roman Gaul, between about 360 and 450 CE, two households of monks lived out the same idea. In both, a monk who was made a bishop went on living as a monk. One grew up around Tours, in the Loire valley. The other grew up on Lérins, a small island off the Mediterranean coast, and in the city of Marseilles. No evidence shows that the two ever wrote to each other.

The northern household began with a soldier named Martin. Before a battle, he asked his commander, Julian Caesar, for his discharge, to serve Christ instead. Years later the people of Tours drew him out of his monastery by a trick and made him their bishop. As bishop, Martin kept the plain habits of a monk, and many of the monks he trained were later made bishops.

After Martin's death, Honoratus took his followers to Lérins. The island stood empty, because it was filthy and no one went near it for fear of snakes. His disciple Hilary preached that Honoratus went in unafraid, with a psalm on his lips, and the snakes gave way. As far as Hilary's sermon can be read, the priesthood he had run from caught up with him on the island. In time he became a bishop himself.

Both households measured themselves against Egypt's monks, in different ways. The south took Egypt's customs as a rule to keep. John Cassian had lived among the Egyptian monks and brought their customs home to Gaul. He changed them only where Gaul's harsh climate or different habits made them impossible or too hard. The north set Martin beside Egypt's hermits. The Tours writer Sulpitius has a traveler just back from Egypt admit that Martin had outdone them all.

From the fathers of Egypt, the south received a goal called purity of heart, and fasting and night prayer were only aids toward it. The monk was kept on course by discretion, the judgment that keeps him between too much and too little. The Egyptian fathers called it the mother of all virtues. On Lérins, Vincent wrote that the true faith is what has been believed everywhere, always, by all.

In his Institutes, Cassian chose not to write up the wonders he had seen, since they teach nothing about how to live. In his Conferences, an Egyptian elder says the fathers never counted a monk good if he showed off his power over demons. Tours told its story through power. Sulpitius tells how Martin brought a dead catechumen, a new believer not yet baptized, back to life. He also tells how the devil once came to Martin dressed as Christ. Martin refused him. He would believe only in a Christ who bore the marks of his wounds.

By Cassian's own account, the south's best-known argument began as a worry at prayer. In Egypt, an old man named Chaeremon told Cassian and his friend Germanus that no one masters the good by effort alone. When Germanus objected, Chaeremon answered with a farmer. A farmer who never plows gets no crop, yet even the hardest worker needs rain he cannot make. The wish to do good, the old man said, comes first from God. That answer grew into a whole Conference on grace and effort.

At Tours, some bishops had opposed Martin's election. Later, at the emperor's court in Trier, Martin once took communion with bishops he had refused, to save lives. He felt it cost him some of his power, and he never attended a synod again. Vincent, by contrast, wrote that the decrees of an ancient general council should be preferred to the rashness and ignorance of a few.

Almost everything known about Tours comes from Sulpitius Severus, who visited Martin there. He was not present for most of what he tells, and says he learned it from Martin and those who lived with him. Knowing his end was near, Martin went to make peace among the quarreling clergy at Condate. As he lay dying, his monks asked to put straw under him. He kept to sackcloth and ashes, so as not to leave them a different example. Almost two thousand monks, it is said, came to his funeral.

dates.display: d. 397, on a peacemaking journey to Condate; a soldier under 'Julian Caesar' in his youth, discharged at a donative; monk 'not far from the town' where Hilary was bishop, then bishop of Tours from an undated election (the monastery across the river founded 'after 371' only on the editorial introduction's word); 'lived sixteen years' after the Treves affair by Gallus's own reckoning

voices.hedge: Almost everything we tell of Martin comes from one writer, Sulpitius Severus, who admired him. Sulpitius visited Martin, but he was not there for most of what he tells. He says he learned it from Martin and from those who lived with him.
voices.text: Martin left the army to serve Christ, telling his commander it was not lawful for him to fight. Sulpitius says he could not easily be drawn out of his monastery. The people of Tours drew him out by a trick and made him their bishop. As bishop, he kept living like a monk, with his brothers two miles outside the city. Sulpitius tells of him healing the sick and raising the dead. Martin felt that power weaken after he once took communion with bishops he had refused, to save lives. After that he stayed away from every gathering of bishops.

dates.display: travelled in Egypt with Germanus in his youth (the interval to his writing not stated in this world's own documents); founded the twin houses at Marseilles c. 415; wrote the Institutes for Castor before 426 and the Conferences in three parts, Part II (to Honoratus and Eucherius) not later than 426; d. c. 435

names.name: Cassian, the founder of the houses at Marseilles

voices.hedge: Cassian never mentions Martin. No story we have shows a monk of Gaul keeping the Egyptian way he wrote down. By his own admission, he could recall no one in our monasteries who kept up the Egyptian perseverance unbroken even for a year.
voices.text: Cassian lived among the monks of Egypt as a young man. Later he founded two houses at Marseilles, one for men and one for women. He wrote down what the Egyptian fathers taught, and in his Institutes he chose not to write up the wonders he had seen. From the fathers he passed on purity of heart as the monk's goal and discretion as his guide. He listed eight faults for a monk to fight in turn. And he wrote down how a question about grace and effort troubled his friend Germanus and him at morning prayer.

dates.display: founded the community on the island of Lerins c. 400-410 (410 on the surviving volume's editorial introduction); addressed by Cassian as a brother presiding over a large monastery, then as a bishop - the see identified as Arles, from 426, only by the editorial apparatus; d. c. 429/430, the year his disciple and successor Hilary preached his life

names.name: Honoratus, the founder of the island
Honoratus of Lerins, later bishop of Arles (d. c. 429/430)

voices.hedge: Almost all we can tell of our founder comes from part of Hilary's funeral sermon. The copy we have of its Latin is hard to read. It tells how he came to the island and was made a priest there. What he or anyone did on the island in between, we cannot tell you.
voices.text: Honoratus took his followers to an island that stood empty, because it was filthy and no one went near it for fear of snakes. His disciple Hilary says he went in unafraid, with a psalm on his lips, and set up a camp of God there. He had run from church office, but on the island, as far as Hilary's sermon can be read, the priesthood caught up with him. In time he became a bishop.

dates.display: writing c. 397 (the Life; Letter III within months of Martin's death) to c. 404-406 (the Dialogues); an Aquitanian 'of an illustrious family' who visited Martin at Tours; birth and death years rest only on the modern editors' disagreeing endnotes and are not asserted

voices.hedge: Nearly everything we know of Tours passes through this one writer. He admired Martin and wrote to make his readers follow him, so he was never a neutral reporter.
voices.text: Sulpitius Severus came from Aquitaine, from a leading family by his editors' account, and he visited Martin at Tours. He wrote Martin's Life so that its readers would be stirred to follow him. He also wrote a letter on Martin's death and the Dialogues, in which his friend Gallus tells more stories of Martin. He says he learned what he tells partly from Martin himself and partly from those who lived with him.

tile.text: Between about 360 and 450 CE, two households of monks in Roman Gaul lived out the same idea. In both, a monk who was made a bishop went on living as a monk. In the Loire valley, the first household grew around Martin, a soldier who had left the army to serve Christ. The people of Tours drew him out of his monastery by a trick and made him their bishop. As bishop, he kept living like a monk. In the years after his death, other monks built houses on Lérins, an island off the Mediterranean coast, and in the city of Marseilles. No evidence shows that the two households ever wrote to each other. One of the southern monks, John Cassian, had lived among the monks of Egypt. He wrote down their teaching for Gaul, changing it only where Gaul's climate or habits made it too hard. He also wrote down a question that troubled him and his friend at prayer. It asked how much of a monk's progress is God's gift and how much his own effort. Another monk, Vincent of Lérins, wrote a short rule for telling true growth in the faith from a corruption dressed up as one.
